turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, September 25. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Netanyahu just triggered a mass walkout at the UN — let's get into it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Hundreds of delegates on their feet and out the door.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Netanyahu's UNGA address Thursday — he called the Gaza genocide allegations "the biggest lie of the century," held up a pager as a prop referencing the 2024 Hezbollah device strikes, and went after New York's own mayor by name, calling Zohran Mamdani antisemitic. Hundreds walked out as he started speaking.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why the direct swing at Mamdani specifically?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Israeli elections are in October, and this reads as campaign positioning dressed up as foreign policy — picking a fight with a sitting US mayor plays to a domestic audience that wants defiance, not diplomacy, right now. The walkout itself is becoming the story more than anything he actually said.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Different continent, actual shooting — Ethiopia's Tigray war is back on.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tigrayan forces seized three federal-controlled airports Wednesday — Mekelle, Shire, and Axum — and took federal police guards prisoner. Ethiopian Airlines suspended all three routes immediately. The TPLF also announced a new alliance with six other armed groups aiming to remove the government in Addis Ababa, and fighting's already spread into the neighboring Afar region.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Wasn't there a peace deal for this exact war?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The 2022 African Union-mediated deal that ended the prior two-year civil war — both sides are now accusing each other of violating it. This is a real risk of that war resuming, not a border skirmish.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What would actually resuming look like, practically?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Federal forces have to decide whether to try retaking three airports by force, which is a real war, or negotiate again from a weaker position than 2022 — the TPLF didn't just seize infrastructure, it built a seven-group coalition explicitly aimed at regime change, which is a materially bigger ask than the last round of fighting. Addis Ababa hasn't said which path it's taking yet. US Business.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Space M&A first — Rocket Lab's Iridium deal just cleared its last hurdle.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Iridium shareholders approved the acquisition today, 99.6% of votes cast in favor. $27 a share cash plus Rocket Lab stock, roughly $8 billion total, closing expected mid-2027. It's one of the largest space-sector deals of the year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the housing data that dropped yesterday is more complicated than the headline.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: August new-home sales jumped 6.4% to 684,000 annualized, the fastest pace of 2026 — but the median new-home price fell 5.8% year-over-year to $393,700. Builders are buying that volume with discounts, not demand.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How widespread is the discounting?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's 8.5 months of supply at the current sales pace, and Parcl Labs says roughly 42% of all active US listings now carry a price cut — a record. Read the volume number as builders clearing inventory at a lower clearing price, not the housing market actually strengthening.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does that change how you'd read the next Fed data point?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It should — a volume beat built on record price-cutting is disinflationary at the household level even while the headline print looks like resilient demand. Anyone reading August's sales number as a strength signal without checking the price line is going to misread the consumer entirely. International.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Caracas at the UN for the first time in years — and there's a hole in the promise.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela's acting president since Maduro's capture and extradition by US forces in January, made her first UN address Thursday. She pledged elections will be held and cited a new political dialogue with opposition sectors — but named no date. First Venezuelan head-of-state UN visit since 2018.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So what's actually changed on the ground?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Nothing verifiable yet — this is an institutional message aimed at legitimacy, with Maduro himself awaiting US trial a few miles away. A promise with no date attached is the header act of this whole segment, and it's not the only one.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: France's the other one — the bond market's genuinely worried now.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The French 10-year OAT yield broke 4.5% Thursday, a level not seen since 2008. The Finance Ministry projects debt hitting a record 119.3% of GDP this year, rising to 121.7% in 2027. PM Lecornu's 2027 draft budget is seen as risking a third government collapse — governments already fell in December 2024 and September 2025 — ahead of the spring presidential election.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A pattern's forming here — nobody's actually closing anything this week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Rodríguez promises elections with no date, Lecornu's budget might not survive its own parliament, and we'll get to a third one when we hit China.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is the France number actually a France problem, or a broader signal?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Watch it as a template — a G7 economy with no majority government and a debt load past 119% of GDP is a preview of how bond markets price political paralysis in any advanced democracy that can't pass a budget. Four-and-a-half percent on a French ten-year would have been unthinkable pre-COVID; now it's a live number with a clear political cause attached, not a mystery move. Markets.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Quiet tape by US standards Thursday — S&P essentially flat at 7,704.13, Nasdaq flat at 26,939.37, Dow off 0.31% to 51,349.98. None of that clears the bar. Everything's on the Markets tab.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What actually moved?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Manila did — the PSEi jumped 1.67% today, snapping a five-day losing streak that had taken it to a ten-month low Thursday. We'll get into why when we hit the Philippines. On the commodity side, WTI's up about 2% to $95.25 a barrel, purely on stalled US-Iran talks — Tehran's naval blockade standoff still hasn't resolved.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the ten-year — still sitting near that nineteen-year high from earlier in the week?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Essentially flat today at 5.12%, but it's holding near the highest level since 2007 after Wednesday's 13-to-16 basis point jump. That's the more durable story than any single day's oil catalyst — a yield floor that high changes mortgage math and corporate refinancing math whether or not it moves again today.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So today's actual signal is a Manila rebound and an oil bid, not anything in New York.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and the interesting read is why the PSEi bounced — foreign buying and bargain-hunting off a genuine multi-month low, with traders citing expectations of lower local gas prices next week easing cost pressure. That's a real technical bounce, not a fundamentals shift, and we'll get into the fundamentals when we get to the Philippines segment properly.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything on gold worth a line?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Down 0.85% to $4,292.90 an ounce — the stronger dollar off that hawkish yield read is doing the work there, not a demand story. Sub-threshold, one line, moving on. Deep Dive.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This week's Economist flags something worth actually chewing on — the backlash against Meta's camera glasses has a name now: "pervert glasses."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a headline doing a lot of work.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's earned it. Meta's camera-equipped Ray-Bans have become a real flashpoint — men secretly filming and harassing women in public, a Dutch privacy group called Bits of Freedom filming Meta's own employees to make the point stick, London pubs and UK courtrooms banning the glasses outright. There's now a lawsuit alleging human annotators reviewed footage of people undressing, using bathrooms, and handling financial documents that got swept into Meta's AI-training pipeline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's Meta actually doing about it, beyond PR?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two real moves. A mandatory firmware update that disables the camera if the privacy LED is tampered with — closing the "cover the light, keep filming" loophole — and a camera-free glasses line launching at this week's Connect conference. That second move is the tell: they're hedging the category, not just defending the current product.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Meanwhile Google and Samsung are walking straight into the same fire.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Their jointly-developed camera glasses launch this fall regardless — betting the category survives the backlash rather than that it needs the same retreat Meta's making. That's the actual fork worth watching: does "ambient AI hardware," which every lab wants as the post-smartphone form factor, standardize on camera-free by default, or does the market just route around the backlash the way Instagram's been playing whack-a-mole with banned accounts?

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which way does the law point?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The UK courtroom bans and Wetherspoons' pub ban are consent-law responses arriving faster than any US regulation — that's usually the leading indicator for how a global product category eventually gets designed. If enough jurisdictions treat always-on cameras on strangers as a default privacy violation rather than an opt-out feature, the hardware roadmap bends around that, not around what Silicon Valley wants to ship.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: First real test of whether ambient AI hardware and consent norms can actually coexist.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the stakes. And it's happening while Meta's simultaneously facing a lawsuit over what its own annotators saw — the backlash isn't hypothetical anymore, there's an actual discovery process running underneath the PR response.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the Dutch privacy group's actual point, filming Meta's own staff?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bits of Freedom turned the camera on Meta's own Amsterdam-area employees deliberately — the argument is that the people building the product wouldn't tolerate being on the other end of it, so the demonstration doubles as both protest and evidence. It's a more effective piece of advocacy than a white paper, because it's the exact scenario the company's own defenders keep calling overblown, played out on people who can't opt out of being recognized as employees of the company that made the glasses.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does the camera-free line actually solve anything, or is it just a release valve?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a release valve dressed as a solution — it doesn't touch the installed base of camera-equipped units already in pubs and on trains, and it doesn't resolve the annotator lawsuit. What it does is give Meta a product to point to in every future regulatory hearing: "we offer a privacy-respecting option," even while the flagship product stays exactly as it is. Energy.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oracle just used a tool nobody's used publicly on an AI campus contract before — force majeure, on its own flagship build.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Force majeure against its own project?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Against its landlord, effectively. Oracle sent a force-majeure notice to Stack Infrastructure, a Blue Owl Capital unit developing Project Jupiter — the Stargate and OpenAI-tied AI campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico. Total buildout's up to $165 billion, and it's about 26% built.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What actually triggered it — a generation problem?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the interesting part — no. The power design is up to 2.45 gigawatts of Bloom Energy solid-oxide fuel cells; Oracle dropped its original gas-turbine plan back in April specifically to dodge the turbine backlog and local opposition. The generation side is fine. The failure point is a single 17-mile gas pipeline feeding those fuel cells.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's wrong with the pipeline?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The New Mexico State Land Office has repeatedly denied right-of-way across state trust land. The route's been redrawn, and the in-service date has already slipped from August 2026 to February 2027. There's a pending air-quality permit ruling due November 23rd that could force a redesign of the entire power system, not just the pipeline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So what does the force-majeure notice actually do for Oracle here?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's not an exit — Oracle isn't walking away as anchor tenant. It's securing the right to delay payments if the campus misses its 2028 open, which shifts the timing and completion risk onto Blue Owl, the landlord, rather than Oracle eating it as offtaker. Oracle shares fell 3 to 5% premarket the same day the notice became public.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is this a one-off, or a template?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: I'd call it the first big public instance of a hyperscaler reaching for force-majeure optionality on an AI-campus contract specifically — worth watching as a template other offtakers copy as pipeline, interconnect, and permitting timelines keep slipping against 2027-28 in-service commitments across the board. It's also the cleanest example yet of the "de-risk generation, get stuck on gas transport" pattern — fuel cells solved the turbine-scarcity risk, they didn't solve the right-of-way risk underneath them.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Different chokepoint, same theme — what's the DOE done on transmission this week?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: DOE announced $1.9 billion in federal funding yesterday for 31 grid-reconductoring projects across 26 states under its SPARK program, expected to add 23 gigawatts of transmission capacity — total project investment $5.25 billion once you add the $3.35 billion in recipient cost-share. Scope is reconductoring or replacing over 1,500 miles of existing lines, plus grid-enhancing tech across roughly 21,000 miles.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why reconductor instead of building new lines?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's the politically and permitting-cheap way to add gigawatt-scale capacity — you're upgrading conductors on existing right-of-way instead of fighting a multi-year new-line siting battle. DOE's own language is explicit about this being faster than greenfield transmission. Put next to Oracle's pipeline problem, it's the same underlying pattern: the last mile of energy delivery — gas transport in Oracle's case, electric transmission here — is where AI-infrastructure timelines actually break, not the generation source itself. Tagalog Vocab.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Panghihimasok.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Panghihimasok — pakikialam o pagsingit sa gawain ng ibang bansa o tao nang wala silang pahintulot o karapatan. Mas may bigat at diplomatic na dating ito kaysa sa payak na "pakikialam," kaya mas madalas itong makikita sa political at foreign-affairs na balita, lalo na kapag may paglabag sa soberanya ng isang bansa.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Malinaw na panghihimasok ang ginawa ng mga barkong Tsino sa loob ng ating teritoryal na karagatan." Karaniwang gamit: panghihimasok sa usaping panloob, dayuhang panghihimasok, walang karapatang manghimasok — lagi itong may implikasyon ng paglabag, hindi lang basta pakikisali.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Susunod — pagbangon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pagbangon — muling pagtayo o paglakas, matapos ang isang pagbagsak o mahirap na yugto. Iba ito sa payak na "pagtaas," na basta pagdami lang — ang "pagbangon" ay may kasamang kuwento ng pagkasubok bago ito, kaya mas may bigat at drama ang dating.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ibigay mo yung halimbawa na maririnig natin mamaya.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Biglaang pagbangon ang naranasan ng PSEi matapos ang limang araw na pagbagsak." Karaniwang pares nito: pagbangon ng ekonomiya, pagbangon mula sa kalamidad, pagbangon ng merkado — parehong salita ngayon, dalawang magkaibang balita sa Philippines segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May bagong panghihimasok ang Tsina sa dagat natin — at malapit lang ito nangyari.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Hinarang ng mga barkong Chinese Coast Guard at PLA Navy ang resupply mission papuntang BRP Sierra Madre sa Ayungin Shoal, Huwebes ng gabi.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ilang barko ang kaharap ng ating convoy?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the record now, in English — per the National Task Force on the West Philippine Sea, three PLA Navy warships and five China Coast Guard vessels, including two Houbei-class missile boats, confronted the convoy roughly 111 kilometers from the shoal. The convoy was the M/V Lapu-Lapu plus three Philippine Navy and Coast Guard support vessels.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How close did this actually get to a real confrontation?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Close enough that a Chinese warship radioed a threat of, quote, compulsory measures. The mission was called off at 11:08 PM for personnel safety. NTF-WPS says the action violates UNCLOS and the 2016 arbitral ruling — this is a fresh incident, not an echo of prior standoffs at the shoal.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang mabuting balita naman — pagbangon ang PSEi ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bumangon nang malakas ang PSEi ngayong Biyernes — plus one point six seven percent, pagkatapos ng limang magkakasunod na araw ng pagbagsak papunta sa sampung-buwang mababa.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: On the record — Wednesday's close was 5,730.02, a fifth straight losing session and a ten-month low. Today's bounce added 95.95 points to close at 5,825.97, on foreign buying and bargain-hunting.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Philstocks is calling it a technical bounce rather than a fundamentals shift — Luis Limlingan at Regina Capital cited expectations of lower local gas prices next week easing cost pressure as the actual trigger. It's a real pagbangon, but a narrow one; nothing's changed about the growth downgrades or the BSP hike calendar we've already covered this week.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does one day of foreign buying tell you anything about sentiment more broadly?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: One day, no — but it's worth watching whether foreign flows keep coming back at these levels, because a ten-month low is exactly the kind of print that either marks a real bottom or gets revisited within weeks. The gas-price expectation driving today's bounce is a real, calendar-dated catalyst, not sentiment alone, which gives it slightly more credibility than a pure technical rebound.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the peso — still sliding, or has it found a floor?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Holding at 62.57, down 0.30% today — a slight firming, a pause after the run of 2026 record lows, the 25th of which hit September 14th at 62.86. No new ground broken either direction. No storm signal today, so weather stays off. Mandarin Vocab.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Today's first word is 搁置, gēzhì — to shelve or set aside an issue, often indefinitely and deliberately.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How's that different from just delaying something?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly the contrast — 拖延, tuōyán, means to delay or procrastinate, and it carries a whiff of avoidance or inefficiency, usually personal. 搁置 is institutional and deliberate — a conscious decision to set something aside, often for an indefinite period, with no implied criticism attached. It's formal, written-register — 书面语 — standard in diplomatic and policy reporting. Common collocations: 搁置争议, shelve a dispute; 搁置计划, shelve a plan; 被搁置的议题, an issue that's been shelved.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Give us the example we'll hear in a minute.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 台湾问题和芯片管制这次被双方搁置，没有列入公报。 The Taiwan issue and chip controls were shelved by both sides this time, and weren't included in the communiqué.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word — 一旦, followed by 就.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 一旦…就 — "once… then." It's an advanced HSK-4 connective marking a single triggering event after which a consequence follows, often irreversibly. Contrast it with 如果…就, rúguǒ…jiù, "if… then," which is a neutral hypothetical that may or may not happen. 一旦…就 implies the trigger is a real, often sudden turning point — heavier stakes once it occurs.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Example.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 一旦台湾问题被重新提起，中美关系就可能急转直下。 Once the Taiwan issue is raised again, US-China relations could take a sharp turn for the worse. Both words, straight into the China story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 台湾问题和芯片管制这次被双方搁置，没有列入公报。 The Taiwan issue and chip controls were shelved by both sides this time, and weren't included in the communiqué.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Walk us through how the actual summit ended.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Xi's Washington visit wrapped Thursday into Friday — a full day of talks plus a state dinner — and the outcome is explicit non-agreement on two fronts: no AI security framework, and no movement on Taiwan, despite everything else on the table. Xi urged the US toward, quote, prudence on Taiwan and a quick end to the Iran war, per Xinhua, and said China's door stays open to US investment, wanting reciprocal treatment for Chinese firms operating there.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 一旦台湾问题被重新提起，中美关系就可能急转直下。 Once the Taiwan issue is raised again, US-China relations could take a sharp turn for the worse.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the honest read on it. The trade truce extension we already know about — pushed to January 10th — is the deliverable both sides could actually agree on. Taiwan arms sales and chip export controls are explicitly separate, unresolved tracks, carved out rather than negotiated.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why carve them out instead of at least addressing them?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because neither side had anything to gain from forcing the harder conversation this week — both needed a deliverable, and trade was the achievable one. 搁置, not resolved. Shelving Taiwan and AI security doesn't make either issue smaller; it just means the pressure under both keeps building while the trade track gets the headline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the summit reads as a win on paper and a punt underneath it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the throughline of the whole morning, honestly — Rodríguez promising elections with no date, Lecornu's budget one no-confidence vote from collapsing, and now Xi and Trump shelving the two hardest issues on their table rather than resolving them. Everyone's buying optionality this week, nobody's closing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does Beijing actually benefit from the shelving, or is it just as stuck as Washington?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Beijing benefits more, on balance — every month Taiwan and AI security stay 搁置 is a month China doesn't have to make a costly concession on either, while the trade track keeps propping up its export engine. Washington gets a calmer news cycle out of the truce; Beijing gets that plus time. It's not a symmetrical shelving, even if it looks like one from the joint statement. Arts.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: New York first — a genuinely overdue reunion at the Met.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous" opens October 4th — the first major New York show devoted to either artist in over twenty years. More than 120 works from over 80 collections, covering both full careers side by side, running through January 31st.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why has it taken this long for a joint show?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Krasner's spent decades overshadowed by Pollock despite a nearly six-decade practice of her own — she outlived him by more than 40 years and kept working the entire time. Putting the two careers in the same rooms, chronologically, is the corrective this show is explicitly built to make.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The auction world's got its own story this week — a genuine estate sale.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sotheby's is previewing the Armand Hammer collection in LA through today, ahead of a November evening sale estimated at $25 to $37 million. Twelve works from the late oil tycoon's collection; proceeds go toward the Armand Hammer Foundation shifting into arts-education grants.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the top lot?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Degas's "Trois danseuses," painted around 1899, estimated at $10 to $15 million. Also Mary Cassatt's 1894 "Summertime," estimated $7 to $10 million, and Renoir's 1888 "Antibes," estimated $2.5 to $3.5 million — a genuinely strong late-19th-century Impressionist trio hitting the block together.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And in books — the Cundill History Prize shortlist just landed.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Eight titles down from roughly 400 submissions for the world's richest nonfiction history prize, $75,000. Jill Lepore's "We The People," a history of the US Constitution, and Jonathan Cheng's "Korean Messiah," on Kim Il Sung and Christianity in North Korea, are the two most attention-grabbing entries. Three finalists get named September 30th, winner announced October 23rd in Montreal.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which one are you actually curious about?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Cheng book — the intersection of state ideology and religious language in North Korea is territory very few historians get real access to write about with primary sources.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The Sotheby's sale has a philanthropy angle too, doesn't it?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It does — proceeds go toward the Armand Hammer Foundation pivoting from its historical medical-research funding toward arts-education grants specifically, so the sale itself is effectively converting an oil fortune's art collection into future arts funding. Worth noting as the estate-sale trend continues reshaping which foundations actually fund the arts going forward. Op-Eds.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Lionel Laurent in Bloomberg Opinion this week — Europe, he argues, is on the menu.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Laurent's borrowing Mark Carney's line — if you're not at the table, you're on the menu — to argue the Trump-Xi truce gives Xi more room to lean on the EU specifically. Europe's exposed on rare-earth dependency and still hasn't decided whether to get tough on Chinese export overcapacity in EVs and industrial goods, all while Washington negotiates policy that affects Europe without actually including it at the table.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The "Europe is a powerless middle power" framing is a recurring genre in this exact column — it understates real EU leverage. Single-market access is a genuine card, the DMA and DSA give Brussels a regulatory stick Washington doesn't have, and tariffs are already imposed on Chinese EVs. Worth asking whether "on the menu" is actually new information this week or a catchy recycling of a standing anxiety.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second piece — the Washington Post on the White House press fight.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Post's editorial board argues Trump can't replace the media he's trying to silence. After banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from pool access, the administration launched a YouTube livestream called Trump TV as a substitute — it flopped — while a "Media Offenders" page on the official White House site names outlets it says publish inaccuracies.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How did the press corps actually respond?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Major networks halted video coverage of the president in solidarity, the banned outlets sued in federal court, and other broadcasters — including Gray TV — declined the White House's invitation to fill CNN's now-vacant pool seat. The Post's argument is that state-run alternative media can't substitute for adversarial press, and that the boycott shows the press corps still has leverage the administration underestimated.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the honest counter to that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Post is a direct party to this fight, not a neutral observer — worth flagging plainly. And most people now get news through podcasts, Substack, and social video anyway, so a White House pool ban may matter far less to actual information flow than it would have a decade ago. This is also a live lawsuit, not a settled outcome — the piece is making a prediction, not reporting a result.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does the failed livestream tell you anything about the actual audience appetite here?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It tells you state-run alternative media doesn't automatically inherit an audience just because the original channel gets cut off — people didn't migrate to Trump TV, they mostly just watched less of any official feed at all. That's a genuinely inconvenient data point for both sides of this argument: it undercuts the administration's bet that it could route around the press, but it also undercuts the Post's implicit assumption that people are hungry for adversarial coverage specifically, rather than just news in general. One Good Thing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Sadie Hutson is twelve years old, from Dobson, North Carolina, and she rescues stuffed animals for a living, more or less — not for money, for kids who've just lost their homes.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How'd she start?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: With her mom, she buys worn, damaged stuffed animals from thrift stores, hand-washes them, repairs them, re-stuffs them, and donates the finished toys to kids who've just lost their homes to fire or other disaster. She's donated 114 restored animals so far to the American Red Cross of North Carolina, after a Red Cross disaster specialist put out a call for comfort-item donations.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Did she want the attention that comes with a story like this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: She was actually shy about the publicity — agreed to it hoping it might inspire other kids to do something similar. A hundred and fourteen toys, each one somebody's first comfort after losing everything else. That's the show. I'm Alex.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And I'm Sam. That's your Friday morning — have a genuinely good weekend, and we'll see you Monday.
